title: Trees & Tries
scopeHtml: Scope: tree recursion, level-order BFS, BST validation, lowest common ancestor, tries.

notes.title: Tree basics and recursion
notes.html:
Idea. A binary tree node has a value and up to two children. Almost every tree problem is solved by recursion that trusts the children: assume the function already works for the left and right subtrees, and combine their answers at the current node.

Recipe for tree recursion.

  1. Base case: an empty node (null) returns the neutral answer (0 for depth, true for validity).
  2. Recurse on left and right.
  3. Combine at the node and return.

Worked example: Maximum depth.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
struct TreeNode { int val; TreeNode *left, *right; TreeNode(int v) : val(v), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {} };

int maxDepth(TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return 0;                                  // base case
    return 1 + max(maxDepth(root->left), maxDepth(root->right));
}
class TreeNode { int val; TreeNode left, right; TreeNode(int v) { val = v; } }

int maxDepth(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return 0;                           // base case
    return 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right));
}
class TreeNode(var `val`: Int) { var left: TreeNode? = null; var right: TreeNode? = null }

fun maxDepth(root: TreeNode?): Int {
    if (root == null) return 0                            // base case
    return 1 + maxOf(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right))
}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def max_depth(root):
    if not root:
        return 0                                          # base case
    return 1 + max(max_depth(root.left), max_depth(root.right))

Complexity. O(n) time (each node once), O(h) stack space where h is the height: O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a skewed one.

Traversal orders. Pre-order (node, left, right) copies a tree; in-order (left, node, right) visits a BST in sorted order; post-order (left, right, node) computes values from children, such as heights and deletions. Level-order uses a queue (next section).

Industry examples. File systems and the DOM are trees; compilers build abstract syntax trees; databases use B-trees; UI frameworks diff virtual trees.

Everyday analogy. A company org chart: the total headcount under a manager is their own plus the totals under each report.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the base case or returning the wrong neutral value.
  • Treating null children as an error instead of the base case.
  • Stack overflow on very deep trees; mention an iterative version with an explicit stack.

notes.title: Tree BFS: level order
notes.html:
Idea. A queue processes nodes level by level. Record the queue size at the start of each loop iteration; that many nodes belong to the current level.

Worked example: Level Order Traversal.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<vector<int>> levelOrder(TreeNode* root) {
    vector<vector<int>> out;
    if (!root) return out;
    queue<TreeNode*> q;
    q.push(root);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int sz = q.size();                                // nodes in this level
        vector<int> level;
        while (sz--) {
            TreeNode* n = q.front(); q.pop();
            level.push_back(n->val);
            if (n->left) q.push(n->left);
            if (n->right) q.push(n->right);
        }
        out.push_back(level);
    }
    return out;
}
List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return out;
    Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(root);
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int sz = q.size();                                // nodes in this level
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < sz; i++) {
            TreeNode n = q.poll();
            level.add(n.val);
            if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
            if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
        }
        out.add(level);
    }
    return out;
}
fun levelOrder(root: TreeNode?): List<List<Int>> {
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    if (root == null) return out
    val q = ArrayDeque<TreeNode>()
    q.addLast(root)
    while (q.isNotEmpty()) {
        val level = mutableListOf<Int>()
        repeat(q.size) {                                  // nodes in this level
            val n = q.removeFirst()
            level.add(n.`val`)
            n.left?.let { q.addLast(it) }
            n.right?.let { q.addLast(it) }
        }
        out.add(level)
    }
    return out
}
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    out = []
    if not root:
        return out
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):                           # nodes in this level
            n = q.popleft()
            level.append(n.val)
            if n.left:
                q.append(n.left)
            if n.right:
                q.append(n.right)
        out.append(level)
    return out

Complexity. O(n) time, O(w) space where w is the maximum width of the tree (up to n/2).

Variants. Right-side view (last node of each level), zig-zag order, average per level, minimum depth (stop at the first leaf), connecting nodes at the same level.

Everyday analogy. Floors of a building: finish everyone on one floor before going to the next.

Common interview traps.

  • Reading q.size() inside the loop condition after pushing children, mixing levels (capture it first).
  • Forgetting the empty tree.

notes.title: Binary search trees
notes.html:
Idea. In a BST, for every node all values in the left subtree are smaller and all in the right subtree are larger. In-order traversal yields sorted values. Search, insert and delete are O(h): O(log n) if balanced.

Worked example: Validate a BST. Checking only left.val < node.val < right.val is wrong; a deep node can violate an ancestor. Pass down the allowed range (low, high) instead.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool isValidBST(TreeNode* n, long long lo = LLONG_MIN, long long hi = LLONG_MAX) {
    if (!n) return true;
    if (n->val <= lo || n->val >= hi) return false;
    return isValidBST(n->left, lo, n->val) && isValidBST(n->right, n->val, hi);
}
boolean isValidBST(TreeNode n, long lo, long hi) {
    if (n == null) return true;
    if (n.val <= lo || n.val >= hi) return false;
    return isValidBST(n.left, lo, n.val) && isValidBST(n.right, n.val, hi);
}
// call: isValidBST(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE)
fun isValidBST(n: TreeNode?, lo: Long = Long.MIN_VALUE, hi: Long = Long.MAX_VALUE): Boolean {
    if (n == null) return true
    if (n.`val` <= lo || n.`val` >= hi) return false
    return isValidBST(n.left, lo, n.`val`.toLong()) && isValidBST(n.right, n.`val`.toLong(), hi)
}
def is_valid_bst(n, lo=float("-inf"), hi=float("inf")):
    if not n:
        return True
    if not (lo < n.val < hi):
        return False
    return is_valid_bst(n.left, lo, n.val) and is_valid_bst(n.right, n.val, hi)

Complexity. O(n) time, O(h) space. Use 64-bit bounds because a node value can equal INT_MIN or INT_MAX.

Self-balancing trees. AVL and red-black trees keep height O(log n) with rotations; Java TreeMap, C++ std::map and many database indexes rely on them.

Industry examples. Ordered maps and sets, range queries ("all keys between a and b"), and database indexes (B-trees generalise BSTs for disk pages).

Everyday analogy. A dictionary's "A to M / N to Z" split repeated at every level.

Common interview traps.

  • Checking only parent-child relations.
  • Using int bounds and failing on Integer.MIN_VALUE nodes.
  • Forgetting duplicates: define whether they go left, right or are disallowed.

notes.title: Lowest common ancestor
notes.html:
Idea. The lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two nodes is the deepest node that has both as descendants. For a general binary tree, recurse: if the current node is p or q return it; the answer is the node where p and q are found in different subtrees.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
TreeNode* lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode* root, TreeNode* p, TreeNode* q) {
    if (!root || root == p || root == q) return root;
    TreeNode* L = lowestCommonAncestor(root->left, p, q);
    TreeNode* R = lowestCommonAncestor(root->right, p, q);
    if (L && R) return root;                              // p and q on different sides
    return L ? L : R;
}
TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (root == null || root == p || root == q) return root;
    TreeNode L = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q);
    TreeNode R = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);
    if (L != null && R != null) return root;              // p and q on different sides
    return L != null ? L : R;
}
fun lowestCommonAncestor(root: TreeNode?, p: TreeNode, q: TreeNode): TreeNode? {
    if (root == null || root === p || root === q) return root
    val l = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q)
    val r = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q)
    if (l != null && r != null) return root               // p and q on different sides
    return l ?: r
}
def lowest_common_ancestor(root, p, q):
    if not root or root is p or root is q:
        return root
    L = lowest_common_ancestor(root.left, p, q)
    R = lowest_common_ancestor(root.right, p, q)
    if L and R:
        return root                                       # p and q on different sides
    return L or R

BST shortcut. In a BST compare values: if both are smaller than the node go left, if both larger go right, else the node is the LCA. O(h) time and O(1) space iteratively.

Complexity. O(n) time and O(h) space for a general tree.

Everyday analogy. The first common manager of two employees in an org chart.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming both nodes exist; clarify.
  • Using the BST shortcut on a non-BST.
  • Comparing values rather than node identity when values can repeat.

notes.title: Tries (prefix trees)
notes.html:
Idea. A trie stores strings character by character along tree edges, so words sharing a prefix share a path. Insert, search and prefix lookups take O(L) for a word of length L, independent of how many words are stored.

Recognise it when: autocomplete, prefix queries, dictionary word search, longest common prefix, word-search boards.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
class Trie {
    struct Node { Node* next[26] = {}; bool end = false; };
    Node* root = new Node();
public:
    void insert(const string& w) {
        Node* n = root;
        for (char c : w) {
            if (!n->next[c - 'a']) n->next[c - 'a'] = new Node();
            n = n->next[c - 'a'];
        }
        n->end = true;
    }
    bool search(const string& w) { Node* n = find(w); return n && n->end; }
    bool startsWith(const string& p) { return find(p) != nullptr; }
private:
    Node* find(const string& s) {
        Node* n = root;
        for (char c : s) { n = n->next[c - 'a']; if (!n) return nullptr; }
        return n;
    }
};
class Trie {
    private static class Node { Node[] next = new Node[26]; boolean end; }
    private final Node root = new Node();

    void insert(String w) {
        Node n = root;
        for (char c : w.toCharArray()) {
            if (n.next[c - 'a'] == null) n.next[c - 'a'] = new Node();
            n = n.next[c - 'a'];
        }
        n.end = true;
    }
    boolean search(String w) { Node n = find(w); return n != null && n.end; }
    boolean startsWith(String p) { return find(p) != null; }
    private Node find(String s) {
        Node n = root;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) { n = n.next[c - 'a']; if (n == null) return null; }
        return n;
    }
}
class Trie {
    private class Node { val next = HashMap<Char, Node>(); var end = false }
    private val root = Node()

    fun insert(w: String) {
        var n = root
        for (c in w) n = n.next.getOrPut(c) { Node() }
        n.end = true
    }
    fun search(w: String) = find(w)?.end == true
    fun startsWith(p: String) = find(p) != null
    private fun find(s: String): Node? {
        var n = root
        for (c in s) n = n.next[c] ?: return null
        return n
    }
}
class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = {}                                    # nested dicts; "$" marks a word end

    def insert(self, w):
        n = self.root
        for c in w:
            n = n.setdefault(c, {})
        n["$"] = True

    def _find(self, s):
        n = self.root
        for c in s:
            if c not in n:
                return None
            n = n[c]
        return n

    def search(self, w):
        n = self._find(w)
        return n is not None and "$" in n

    def starts_with(self, p):
        return self._find(p) is not None

Complexity. O(L) per operation; memory O(total characters × alphabet) with arrays, less with hash maps.

Industry examples. Autocomplete and spell-check, IP routing tables (longest-prefix match uses a radix trie), and T9/keyboard prediction.

Everyday analogy. A phone book where you flip letter by letter, narrowing the entries with each letter.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing "is a prefix" with "is a stored word" (the end flag).
  • Fixed 26-slot arrays on input with uppercase or Unicode letters.
  • High memory: use hash maps or compressed (radix) tries.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Tree problems are recursion with a base case at null, trusting children and combining at the node; cost is O(n) time and O(height) stack. BFS with a queue and a per-level size handles level-order problems. A BST is valid only if every node falls inside an inherited (low, high) range; in-order traversal of a BST is sorted. LCA recurses and returns the node where the two targets split, or uses value comparisons in a BST. A trie gives O(L) prefix operations for autocomplete and dictionary problems; track the end-of-word flag.

questions.promptHtml: What is the complexity of a recursive tree traversal in time and space, and what changes for a skewed tree?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates forget the hidden recursion-stack cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Time is O(n) because each node is visited once. Extra space is the recursion depth, O(h): O(log n) for a balanced tree but O(n) for a skewed one, which can overflow the stack.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
For very deep trees convert to an iterative traversal with an explicit stack or use Morris traversal for O(1) extra space. Pre-order copies a tree, in-order sorts a BST, post-order computes values from children.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int maxDepth(TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return 0;
    return 1 + max(maxDepth(root->left), maxDepth(root->right));
}
int maxDepth(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return 0;
    return 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right));
}
fun maxDepth(root: TreeNode?): Int {
    if (root == null) return 0
    return 1 + maxOf(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right))
}
def max_depth(root):
    if not root:
        return 0
    return 1 + max(max_depth(root.left), max_depth(root.right))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the base case.
  • Ignoring stack overflow for a degenerate tree of 10^5 nodes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Iterative version? → Explicit stack for DFS or queue for BFS.
  2. Diameter of a tree? → Post-order: longest path through a node is left height + right height.
  3. Is a tree balanced? → Post-order returning height or -1 for imbalance.

sections.html: Senior mentions stack depth limits, iterative and Morris traversals.

questions.promptHtml: Return the level-order traversal of a binary tree as a list of levels. How do you know where a level ends?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The base BFS template with a standard trick.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use a queue. At the start of each outer iteration record the queue size; that many nodes form the current level. Pop exactly that many, add their values, and enqueue their children. O(n) time, O(width) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Capturing the size before the inner loop is essential because the queue grows while you push children. Variants (right-side view, zig-zag, minimum depth) only change what you do inside the inner loop.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<vector<int>> levelOrder(TreeNode* root) {
    vector<vector<int>> out;
    if (!root) return out;
    queue<TreeNode*> q;
    q.push(root);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int sz = q.size();
        vector<int> level;
        while (sz--) {
            TreeNode* n = q.front(); q.pop();
            level.push_back(n->val);
            if (n->left) q.push(n->left);
            if (n->right) q.push(n->right);
        }
        out.push_back(level);
    }
    return out;
}
List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return out;
    Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(root);
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int sz = q.size();
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < sz; i++) {
            TreeNode n = q.poll();
            level.add(n.val);
            if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
            if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
        }
        out.add(level);
    }
    return out;
}
fun levelOrder(root: TreeNode?): List<List<Int>> {
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    if (root == null) return out
    val q = ArrayDeque<TreeNode>()
    q.addLast(root)
    while (q.isNotEmpty()) {
        val level = mutableListOf<Int>()
        repeat(q.size) {
            val n = q.removeFirst()
            level.add(n.`val`)
            n.left?.let { q.addLast(it) }
            n.right?.let { q.addLast(it) }
        }
        out.add(level)
    }
    return out
}
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    out = []
    if not root:
        return out
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            n = q.popleft()
            level.append(n.val)
            if n.left:
                q.append(n.left)
            if n.right:
                q.append(n.right)
        out.append(level)
    return out

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading the queue size after pushing children, which mixes levels.
  • Forgetting the empty tree.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Right-side view? → Last node of each level.
  2. Zig-zag order? → Reverse every other level.
  3. BFS vs DFS memory? → BFS holds a level (up to n/2 nodes); DFS holds a root-to-leaf path.

questions.promptHtml: Validate whether a binary tree is a binary search tree. Why is checking only each node's children wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A classic trap with a plausible but incorrect solution.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Pass an allowed range (low, high) down the recursion: the left child must lie in (low, node) and the right child in (node, high). Checking only left < node < right misses cases where a deeper node violates an ancestor's constraint. O(n) time, O(h) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Alternatively do an in-order traversal and verify the sequence is strictly increasing. Use 64-bit bounds because node values can equal the 32-bit extremes.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool isValidBST(TreeNode* n, long long lo = LLONG_MIN, long long hi = LLONG_MAX) {
    if (!n) return true;
    if (n->val <= lo || n->val >= hi) return false;
    return isValidBST(n->left, lo, n->val) && isValidBST(n->right, n->val, hi);
}
boolean isValidBST(TreeNode n, long lo, long hi) {
    if (n == null) return true;
    if (n.val <= lo || n.val >= hi) return false;
    return isValidBST(n.left, lo, n.val) && isValidBST(n.right, n.val, hi);
}
fun isValidBST(n: TreeNode?, lo: Long = Long.MIN_VALUE, hi: Long = Long.MAX_VALUE): Boolean {
    if (n == null) return true
    if (n.`val` <= lo || n.`val` >= hi) return false
    return isValidBST(n.left, lo, n.`val`.toLong()) && isValidBST(n.right, n.`val`.toLong(), hi)
}
def is_valid_bst(n, lo=float("-inf"), hi=float("inf")):
    if not n:
        return True
    if not (lo < n.val < hi):
        return False
    return is_valid_bst(n.left, lo, n.val) and is_valid_bst(n.right, n.val, hi)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Parent-child-only comparison.
  • int bounds failing on INT_MIN or INT_MAX nodes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Duplicates allowed? → Decide a convention (for example allow on the right) and adjust the strictness.
  2. Kth smallest in a BST? → In-order traversal, stop at k.
  3. Convert a sorted array to a balanced BST? → Pick the middle as root and recurse.

sections.html: Senior gives both the range and in-order solutions and discusses duplicates.

questions.promptHtml: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a binary tree. How does it simplify in a BST?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests recursion where the answer is "where the paths split".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Recurse; if the node is null or equals p or q, return it. If both the left and right recursive calls return non-null, the current node is the split point and the LCA; otherwise return whichever side is non-null. O(n) time, O(h) space. In a BST compare values and walk down: if both are smaller go left, if both larger go right, else you are at the LCA.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The function returns "the first target found in this subtree" or the LCA if both were found. This relies on both nodes being present; otherwise verify existence separately.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
TreeNode* lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode* root, TreeNode* p, TreeNode* q) {
    if (!root || root == p || root == q) return root;
    TreeNode* L = lowestCommonAncestor(root->left, p, q);
    TreeNode* R = lowestCommonAncestor(root->right, p, q);
    if (L && R) return root;
    return L ? L : R;
}
TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (root == null || root == p || root == q) return root;
    TreeNode L = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q);
    TreeNode R = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);
    if (L != null && R != null) return root;
    return L != null ? L : R;
}
fun lowestCommonAncestor(root: TreeNode?, p: TreeNode, q: TreeNode): TreeNode? {
    if (root == null || root === p || root === q) return root
    val l = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q)
    val r = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q)
    if (l != null && r != null) return root
    return l ?: r
}
def lowest_common_ancestor(root, p, q):
    if not root or root is p or root is q:
        return root
    L = lowest_common_ancestor(root.left, p, q)
    R = lowest_common_ancestor(root.right, p, q)
    if L and R:
        return root
    return L or R

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the BST shortcut on a general tree.
  • Comparing values where duplicates make identity necessary.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Many LCA queries? → Binary lifting or Euler tour plus sparse table for O(log n) or O(1) queries.
  2. Nodes might not exist? → Return a found-both flag.
  3. Distance between two nodes? → depth(p) + depth(q) - 2·depth(LCA).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions preprocessing for repeated queries.

questions.promptHtml: Implement a trie with insert, search and startsWith. When would you choose it over a hash set?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests data-structure design and prefix-problem recognition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each node holds children keyed by character and an end-of-word flag. Insert, search and prefix checks take O(L) for a string of length L. Choose a trie over a hash set when you need prefix queries (autocomplete, prefix counts, longest common prefix), since a hash set can only answer exact membership.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Memory is the weak point: a 26-array per node wastes space for sparse data; hash-map children or radix (compressed) tries reduce it. Search must check the end flag; startsWith does not.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
class Trie {
    struct Node { Node* next[26] = {}; bool end = false; };
    Node* root = new Node();
public:
    void insert(const string& w) {
        Node* n = root;
        for (char c : w) {
            if (!n->next[c - 'a']) n->next[c - 'a'] = new Node();
            n = n->next[c - 'a'];
        }
        n->end = true;
    }
    bool search(const string& w) { Node* n = find(w); return n && n->end; }
    bool startsWith(const string& p) { return find(p) != nullptr; }
private:
    Node* find(const string& s) {
        Node* n = root;
        for (char c : s) { n = n->next[c - 'a']; if (!n) return nullptr; }
        return n;
    }
};
class Trie {
    private static class Node { Node[] next = new Node[26]; boolean end; }
    private final Node root = new Node();
    void insert(String w) {
        Node n = root;
        for (char c : w.toCharArray()) {
            if (n.next[c - 'a'] == null) n.next[c - 'a'] = new Node();
            n = n.next[c - 'a'];
        }
        n.end = true;
    }
    boolean search(String w) { Node n = find(w); return n != null && n.end; }
    boolean startsWith(String p) { return find(p) != null; }
    private Node find(String s) {
        Node n = root;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) { n = n.next[c - 'a']; if (n == null) return null; }
        return n;
    }
}
class Trie {
    private class Node { val next = HashMap<Char, Node>(); var end = false }
    private val root = Node()
    fun insert(w: String) {
        var n = root
        for (c in w) n = n.next.getOrPut(c) { Node() }
        n.end = true
    }
    fun search(w: String) = find(w)?.end == true
    fun startsWith(p: String) = find(p) != null
    private fun find(s: String): Node? {
        var n = root
        for (c in s) n = n.next[c] ?: return null
        return n
    }
}
class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = {}

    def insert(self, w):
        n = self.root
        for c in w:
            n = n.setdefault(c, {})
        n["$"] = True

    def _find(self, s):
        n = self.root
        for c in s:
            if c not in n:
                return None
            n = n[c]
        return n

    def search(self, w):
        n = self._find(w)
        return n is not None and "$" in n

    def starts_with(self, p):
        return self._find(p) is not None

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning true from search for a mere prefix.
  • Assuming lowercase letters only.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Autocomplete suggestions? → Walk to the prefix node, then DFS collecting words.
  2. Memory heavy? → Compressed radix trie or a double-array trie.
  3. Delete a word? → Unset the flag and prune childless nodes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior discusses memory layout and compressed tries for production autocomplete.

questions.contextHtml: A search box must suggest the 5 most popular queries for a typed prefix within 20 ms. There are 50 million distinct queries and prefix lookups arrive at 30,000 requests per second. A prototype scans a sorted list for every keystroke and takes 400 ms.
questions.promptHtml: How would you design the suggestion lookup?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: A SQL LIKE 'prefix%' per keystroke with an ORDER BY on popularity.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How fresh must popularity be? Is personalisation required? Languages and typo tolerance? Memory budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache the most frequent prefixes in memory and cap suggestions at 5.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Scanning the whole list is O(n) per request; sorting by popularity each time is wasteful.
  4. How I'd verify: Benchmark lookup time per prefix and memory per structure.
  5. Root cause: No index on prefixes and no precomputed ranking.
  6. Fix: Build a trie (or radix trie) where each node stores the top 5 completions for its prefix, precomputed offline from query logs. A lookup walks L characters and returns the stored list in O(L). Rebuild periodically (for example hourly) and swap atomically; keep a small realtime overlay for trending queries.
  7. Prevention: Monitor latency, hit rate and index freshness; test against abusive prefixes.
  8. Trade-offs: Storing top-k at every node costs memory (compress, store only on nodes that matter, or shard by first characters); fuzzy matching needs edit-distance structures or an inverted index.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Memory too large for one machine? → Shard by prefix across servers and cache hot prefixes at the edge.
  • Typos? → Fuzzy search with n-grams or a BK-tree on top of the trie.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Precomputing top-k per trie node cut suggestion latency from hundreds of milliseconds to about 2 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: database scan.
  • Hire: trie with top-k per node.
  • Strong hire: offline build, atomic swap, sharding and memory/fuzzy trade-offs.
